Canberra Drive EC site draws most bids in eight years, sets new record land price of $825 psf ppr
article:
A consortium comprising Santarli Realty, Heeton Holdings, Kay Lim Holdings and Sunray Group Holdings has emerged as the top bidder for an executive condominium (EC) site at Canberra Drive, with an offer of $163.9 million, or about $825 psf per plot ratio (ppr).

The 99-year leasehold Government Land Sale (GLS) site attracted 13 bids when its tender closed on Oct 1 — far exceeding analysts’ expectations of three to five bids and marking the strongest turnout for an EC land tender in eight years.

The top bid also sets a new benchmark for EC land prices, Huttons Asia CEO Mark Yip says.

It exceeds the previous record of $794 psf ppr set by Sim Lian Group for the second EC site at Woodlands Drive 17, when that tender closed on Jan 13.

The strong competition for the Canberra Drive site comes despite cooling measures announced in May that tightened several rules governing new EC purchases.

The Santarli-Kay Lim-Heeton-Sunray consortium’s bid was 2.74% higher than the second-highest offer of $159.43 million, or $803 psf ppr, submitted by a joint venture between TID and Hong Leong Group.

The third-highest bid stood at $798 psf ppr from a consortium comprising Apex Asia Development, BHCC Development, and HDB Development.

Other bids included $770 psf ppr from a joint venture between Chan Rong Fen Construction and BS Capital, $735 psf ppr from City Developments Ltd (CDL), and $710 psf ppr from Kheng Leong.

The lowest bid, submitted by Sim Lian Group, stood at $71.72 million, or $361 psf ppr, putting the spread between the highest and lowest bids at 128.5%.

Recent measures

Yip attributes the wide range of bids partly to uncertainty over how recent policy changes will affect demand for new ECs.

Measures announced on May 8 included extending the minimum occupation period for new ECs to 10 years from five, removing the Deferred Payment Scheme, and increasing the allocation priority for first-timer households.

Under the revised EC framework, first-timer allocation will increase from 70% to 90%, while the priority period will extend from one month to two years. "This means that second-timer households would generally account for only 10% of the initial allocation during this period," notes Mohan Sandrasegeran, SRI head of research and data analytics.

The monthly household income ceiling for EC buyers was subsequently raised to $18,000 in August, a move that some developers may have viewed as widening the pool of eligible buyers, Huttons' Yip adds.

Despite the tighter rules, the tender drew more than double the bids analysts generally expected.

The mix of bidders also included developers that have been less active in the EC market in recent years, alongside established EC players. Master Contract Services, for instance, previously developed The Amore EC in Punggol with Keong Hong after winning the site in 2013.

The Canberra Drive tender also attracted a bid from a joint venture between Chan Rong Fen Building Construction and BS Capital Group, which appears to be making its first foray into an EC land tender.

The relatively smaller scale of the Canberra Drive EC site may have given developers greater confidence in assessing the implications of the revised EC framework, says Sandrasegeran.

Highest bid in eight years

The 13 bids are the most received for an EC site since 2018, when the Sumang Walk site in Punggol attracted a record 17 offers. Two years earlier, the Anchorvale Lane site, later developed into Rivercove Residences , drew 16 bids.

The 291,235 sq ft Sumang Walk site was awarded to a joint venture between CDL and TID — a joint venture between Hong Leong Holdings and Mitsui Fudosan — for $509.37 million, or $583 psf ppr.

The site was subsequently developed into the 820-unit Piermont Grand , which launched in July 2019 at an average price of about $1,080 psf, making it the first EC to launch above the $1,000 psf mark. The project was completed in 2023.

The latest tender signals continued developer appetite for EC sites even as the government has sought to temper demand in the segment.

Sixth EC site in the Canberra-Sembawang area

The Canberra Drive site was launched for tender on May 26. Spanning 124,167 sq ft, it can yield about 185 homes, making it a relatively small EC project.

The previous EC site released in the Canberra-Sembawang area was at Sembawang Road. The site, which can yield about 265 units, drew four bids when its tender closed in 2025. It was awarded in September that year to Oriental Pacific Development for $197.8 million, or $692 psf ppr.

The Canberra Drive plot marks the sixth EC site to be released in the Canberra area. Completed EC projects in the neighbourhood include the 638-unit The Brownstone , launched in July 2015; the 632-unit The Visionaire , launched in April 2016; the 496-unit Parc Canberra , launched in February 2020; and the 413-unit Provence Residence , launched in May 2021. The Sembawang Road site awarded in 2025 is the fifth.

The site is about a five-minute walk from Canberra MRT Station. Schools within 1km include Sembawang Primary School and Wellington Primary School.

At a top bid land rate of $825 psf ppr, PropNex head of research and content Wong Siew Ying projects the average selling price of the new EC project may be around $1,900 psf.

The tender for another EC plot in Admiralty Walk will close on Dec 17, and it will provide "a second reading of how the market values EC land under the new measures". The site is likely to yield about 450 units and is farther from an MRT station, notes Wong.

“The strong turnout this time does not mean caution has been thrown to the wind for future EC tenders," says Eugene Lim, ERA Singapore key executive officer. Developer participation will still likely hinge on upcoming supply and site-specific attributes, alongside the new EC rules.

For instance, in the North, Wynwood Grand – alongside upcoming projects at Sembawang Road, Woodlands Drive 17, Miltonia Close, and Canberra Drive itself – could add about 1,860 units to the EC pipeline. "As such, developers are likely to keep this supply wave firmly in mind before throwing their hat in the ring for the Admiralty Walk EC site," says Lim.

“Rising interest rates and a softer domestic job market could likewise dampen homebuying sentiment, which may encourage developers to exercise greater restraint at upcoming tenders.”

title: Five-room flat at SkyTerrace @ Dawson sold for $1.6 mil, setting islandwide HDB resale psf record of $1,502
article:
A five-room flat at 91 Dawson Road , part of SkyTerrace @ Dawson in Queenstown, was sold for $1.6 million ($1,502 psf) in September 2026. This is the highest psf recorded for an HDB resale flat in Singapore. The price is also the highest paid for a flat in the block.

Located on the 37th to 39th storeys, the 1,065 sq ft flat has a remaining lease of about 89 years, with the lease commencing in 2016.

The transaction surpasses the previous psf high of $1,501, set by a four-room flat at 1C Cantonment Road , part of The Pinnacle@Duxton , in March 2025 (see Table 1). Eight of the other nine transactions in the top 10 were at The Pinnacle@Duxton development along Cantonment Road.

The subject flat is one of 12 HDB resale flats that have transacted at $1.6 million or more so far in 2026.

In Queenstown, the previous psf record was $1,455, set by another five-room flat in the same block in March 2026 (see Table 2). That flat sold for $1.55 million.

Four of the five highest HDB resale transactions by psf in Queenstown were at SkyTerrace @ Dawson. The remaining transaction was a four-room flat at 94 Dawson Road, part of the neighbouring SkyParc @ Dawson , sold for $1.388 million ($1,417 psf) in September 2026.

SkyTerrace @ Dawson also holds the town's highest resale price of $1.7 million ($1,295 psf), set by a larger five-room flat in February 2026 , EdgeProp Singapore reported. The subject flat sold for $100,000 less, but at $207 more per sq ft. This suggests demand for units in the development remains strong, with buyers willing to pay more per sq ft for the smaller unit.

The subject flat's high psf could be attributed to its high floor and its location in the mature Queenstown estate. It is within a 1km walk of Queenstown MRT Station (see Map 1). The flat's relatively long remaining lease of about 89 years may have also supported the price.

The development's award-winning design could be another factor. SkyTerrace @ Dawson was named Design of the Year at the 2016 President's Design Award. HDB had commissioned private firm SCDA Architects in 2008 to design the development. Its five blocks of 40 to 43 storeys feature sky gardens on the upper floors and paired units for multi-generational living.

The development sits beside the Alexandra Canal Linear Park, a park connector linking Queenstown MRT Station to Tanglin Road. Other amenities nearby include a FairPrice supermarket at Dawson Place and a Sheng Siong supermarket, both open 24 hours. Queenstown Primary School is within 1km.

Nearby on Margaret Drive, a GuocoLand-Hong Leong consortium was awarded a government land sale (GLS) site for $497 million ($1,154 psf ppr) in 2024. The 462-unit Penrith condo on the site sold 97% of its units on launch day in October 2025, at $2,435 psf to $3,088 psf.

title: Coliwoo sells two River Valley properties for $45.5 mil in three-year leaseback deal
article:
Singapore-listed co-living operator Coliwoo Holdings has agreed to sell two freehold properties in River Valley to Qing Feng Construction for a total of $45.5 million, while continuing to operate them under a three-year leaseback arrangement, the company said in an Oct 1 SGX announcement.

The properties are located at 298 and 288 River Valley Road, respectively. Qing Feng will acquire the companies holding the two properties for $14 million and $31.5 million, respectively.

Qing Feng Construction is a Singapore construction company whose projects span the residential, commercial and industrial sectors. The company has operated in Singapore for more than two decades and undertakes general building, design-and-build and civil engineering works.

Upon completion of the transaction, a Coliwoo subsidiary will lease both properties from the new owner for three years, allowing the group to continue operating them under the Coliwoo brand without disruption.

The transaction follows Coliwoo's move in March to put seven freehold hospitality and living properties on the market for a combined $218.5 million as part of its capital recycling strategy.

The portfolio included three properties at 268, 288 and 298 River Valley Road, which together comprise 73 keys and were marketed at a combined guide price of $78.5 million.

Coliwoo said the latest disposal will similarly allow it to unlock value from the two properties, recycle capital into higher-yielding growth opportunities and strengthen its balance sheet through debt reduction.

After repaying borrowings secured on the properties, transaction-related expenses, and other completion adjustments, Coliwoo expects to receive net proceeds of about $18.7 million. The proceeds will be used for general corporate and working capital purposes, including funding existing and future projects and reducing debt

As the $45.5 million consideration represents 21.7% of Coliwoo's market capitalisation under SGX listing rules, the disposal is considered a major transaction and requires shareholder approval at an extraordinary general meeting.

Sophia Lim, director of capital markets at Cushman & Wakefield, brokered the sale. "The sale of these River Valley serviced apartments reflects the continued strength of investor interest in Singapore's living sector, particularly for well-located and operationally established accommodation assets," she says.

title: Freehold project Peach Garden leads weekly condo resale gains with $3.6 mil profit
article:
A four-bedroom apartment at Peach Garden in Marine Parade topped the list of profitable condo resale transactions during the week of Sept 15 to 22.

The seller of the 2,766 sq ft apartment netted a profit of $3.62 million (244.6%) when it fetched $5.1 million ($1,844 psf) on Sept 17. It was purchased for $1.48 million ($535 psf) in July 2003, resulting in an annualised gain of 5.5% over a holding period of about 23 years.

Based on caveats lodged, the transaction is Peach Garden’s most profitable deal thus far. It inches past the previous record set in January 2012, when a 5,231 sq ft penthouse changed hands for $6.85 million. The seller scored a gain of $3.6 million on the deal, having bought the unit in April 2004 for $3.25 million.

Completed in 1975, Peach Garden is a freehold development off Meyer Road in District 15. It comprises two blocks with 72 apartments — predominantly four-bedders spanning 2,766 sq ft. There are also penthouses measuring 5,231 sq ft.

Aside from the Sept 17 deal, there have been three other resale transactions at Peach Garden this year, one of which was profitable. On April 6, another 2,766 sq ft apartment was sold for $5.12 million, reaping a profit of $1.13 million.

The second most profitable resale during the week was logged at freehold condo The Botanic on Lloyd in District 9.

A four-bedder on the fifth floor scored a profit of $3.25 million (153%) when it was sold on Sept 18 for $5.38 million, or $2,074 psf. That works out to a 4.2% gain on an annualised basis over a holding period of almost 23 years. The 2,594 sq ft apartment was originally purchased for $2.13 million ($820 psf) in December 2003.

This is the second-highest gain made on an apartment at The Botanic on Lloyd. It is lower than the $4.15 million record profit set four years ago by the sale of a 3,584 sq ft four-bedder. That apartment — purchased for $2.73 milion in 2005 — changed hands for around $6.88 million in January 2022.

The Botanic on Lloyd is a 66-unit boutique development located along Lloyd Road, off Oxley Road in the River Valley area. Completed in 2006, the development comprises three- to four-bedroom units ranging from 1,485 to 3,584 sq ft. It also includes six three-storey townhouses spanning 4,058 to 4,446 sq ft.

URA data compiled by EdgeProp Research shows that The Botanic on Lloyd recorded just one other resale deal this year, which was also in the black. A 3,488 sq ft, four-bedroom apartment fetched about $7.48 million on April 7, reaping a gain of $1.68 million.

At the other end of the spectrum , the steepest loss among this week’s most unprofitable condo resales involved a three-bedder at Suites at Orchard .

The transaction left the seller $432,000 in the red, translating to an annualised loss of 1.1% over a 12.5-year holding period. The 1,582 sq ft apartment on the seventh floor changed hands for $2.79 million ($1,762 psf) on Sept 17, below its previous purchase price of $3.22 million ($2,049 psf).

Located along Handy Road, Suites at Orchard is a 99-year leasehold development completed in 2014. It houses 118 apartments across one- to three-bedroom types, with sizes ranging from 548 to 2,196 sq ft.

The Sept 17 deal marks the first transaction at the project this year, going by caveats lodged. In 2025, Suites at Orchard logged five resale deals. Of these, four were unprofitable, incurring losses ranging from $2,000 to $239,000.

title: Resale two-bedder drives Park Infinia at Wee Nam to record high of $2,775 psf
article:
Park Infinia at Wee Nam — a freehold condo in District 11 — emerged the top performer among private non-landed residential developments that set new psf-price peaks from Sept 15 to 22.

The development set a new record of $2,775 psf with the sale of an 850 sq ft, two-bedroom unit on the 22nd floor for $2.36 million on Sept 18. It surpasses the previous price high of $2,691 psf, set in December 2025 when another 850 sq ft unit fetched $2.29 million.

Park Infinia at Wee Nam is a 486-unit condo located along Lincoln Road. Completed in 2008, it comprises one- to four-bedders ranging from 560 to 2,002 sq ft. There are also penthouses of 2,702 to 3,315 sq ft.

Based on caveats compiled by EdgeProp Singapore , Park Infinia at Wee Nam has an average resale price of $2,499 psf, going by transactions over the last 12 months.

This is higher than other freehold developments within a 1km vicinity, such as The Lincoln Modern and The Linc, which average at $1,986 psf and $2,178 psf, respectively.

Still, Park Infinia at Wee Nam’s average resale price remains below that of Viva , a newer freehold condo in the area, which recorded an average of $2,788 psf.

Second among the week’s top project highs was 99-year leasehold condo Jadescape .

The sale of a 904 sq ft, three-bedroom unit scored a new price peak of $2,710 psf for the project when it fetched $2.45 million on Sept 21.

That is the first time a unit at Jadescape has transacted above the $2,700 psf threshold. It edges past the condo’s former record of $2,652 psf set almost two months prior on July 6, when a 1,152 sq ft three-bedder was sold for around $3.06 million.

Located at the junction of Marymount Road and Shufu Road, Jadescape is a 1,206-unit development completed in 2022. It comprises seven residential towers housing one- to five-bedders sized between 527 and 4,230 sq ft.

The condo has seen a high volume of units changing hands, with a total of 43 resale deals so far this year. Excluding the Sept 21 and July 6 deals, the units, which measure between 527 and 2,099 sq ft, fetched prices ranging from $1,856 psf to $2,650 psf.

District 11 development The Lincoln Residences also hit a new psf-price high during the week. A 1,841 sq ft four-bedder on the 23rd floor was sold for $4.55 million on Sept 21. That set a fresh price benchmark of $2,472 psf at the freehold development.

It beats the project’s previous peak of $2,323 psf that was recorded from the resale of a 1,410 sq ft, three-bedroom unit on the 23rd storey for $3.28 million in January last year.

Completed in 2011, The Lincoln Residences is located along Surrey Road. It comprises 99 units, with layouts ranging from three- to four-bedroom apartments spanning 1,281 to 2,573 sq ft. There are also two five-bedroom duplex penthouses measuring 3,229 and 3,337 sq ft.

Novena MRT Station is located within a nine-minute walk from the development.

The highest quantum recorded at the condo was for the 3,229 sq ft duplex penthouse unit when it changed hands for around $5.3 million ($1,640 psf) in January 2013.

No psf-price lows were recorded for the week.

title: Katrina Group unveils newly renovated ST Signature Midtown at Beach Road
article:
ST Signature, the hospitality brand of Katrina Group, has opened its newly renovated co-living hotel, ST Signature Midtown.

Located at 85 Beach Road, the property comprises 38 en suite rooms across four room types, from Cabin M to Cabin XL. The largest rooms can accommodate up to four guests.

ST Signature Midtown offers overnight stays, as well as flexible stay durations and time blocks, which could appeal to “tourists with gaps between flights or itineraries”, said the group.

Guests will have access to high-speed internet and 24-hour online chat support. They can also manage their stay through ST Signature’s smart self-check-in system, including making bookings and payments, and accessing their rooms using a digital key.

“The way people travel and stay has changed, with guests placing greater value on convenience and flexibility,” said Andreas Lorenz, COO of Katrina Group.

The newly refreshed property features artwork in its shared kitchen and communal spaces designed by Singapore-based artist Sean Dunston, which draw inspiration from Beach Road's cinema past.

It is located within a six- to eight-minute walk from lifestyle and dining amenities at Bugis Junction , Bugis+ , and Haji Lane .

Alan Goh, executive chairman and CEO of Katrina Group, said: “Midtown gives us an opportunity to bring the ST Signature experience to a particularly vibrant part of Singapore, where guests can have a private space of their own while being close to the energy of Bugis and the surrounding neighbourhoods.”

title: Navigating a changing en bloc landscape: What the new collective sale framework could mean
article:
Singapore’s parliament passed the Land Titles (Strata) (Amendment) Bill 2026 on Sept 8, lowering the consent thresholds for collective sales of older developments. The changes aim to support the rejuvenation of ageing developments and optimise land use, while strengthening safeguards for owners who do not wish to sell.

The amendments have yet to take effect. They will come into force on a date appointed by the minister and notified in the government gazette.

One of the most significant changes is the introduction of lower collective sale consent thresholds for older developments. Developments aged between 40 and 59 years will require consent from at least 70% of owners by the relevant statutory measures, down from the existing 80%, while developments aged 60 years and above will see the threshold reduced further to 65%.

The existing thresholds will remain unchanged for developments under 40 years old: 90% for those less than 10 years old and 80% for those aged 10 to 39 years.

The revised thresholds are especially relevant for ageing developments, where securing sufficient owner support can be difficult. The challenge can be greater in large estates with many owners, whose differing financial circumstances, housing needs and price expectations can make consensus harder to reach.

However, the amendments are not simply a relaxation of collective sale rules. The revised framework also tightens safeguards around the process: a higher level of support is needed to initiate a collective sale attempt, owners have less time to secure the required consent, and an unsuccessful attempt triggers a longer restriction period before another attempt can be made.

The changes aim to balance the rejuvenation of ageing developments with greater protection for owners who wish to stay in their homes.

Beyond the revised consent thresholds, the amendments make several changes to the collective sale process.

The initial support needed to convene a general meeting to form a collective sale committee rises to 35%. The period for collecting signatures on the collective sale agreement is halved from 12 months to six, and the restriction period after an unsuccessful attempt is extended from two years to three for attempts made under the new framework.

ABSD changes give developers more time on large en bloc sites

The collective sale amendments follow another significant policy change affecting large en bloc sites.

On July 28, the government announced revisions to the additional buyer’s stamp duty (ABSD) remission framework for housing developers undertaking large-scale en bloc redevelopments.

For qualifying sites purchased from July 29, developers of projects yielding 700 to 1,399 residential units will have six years to complete and sell all units, up from 5.5 years.

Sites yielding at least 1,400 units, termed “mega sites”, will have seven years. However, developers must sell at least half of the units by the end of the sixth year.

For large and mega sites to qualify, the redevelopment must also yield at least 1.5 times the number of residential units in the existing development. The commencement timeline remains at 2.5 years.

The revisions recognise the longer planning, construction and sales periods that large-scale redevelopments can require. A project of 1,400 or more homes involves materially different development and sales considerations from a conventional project of a few hundred units.

Addressing both sides of the collective sale equation

Taken together, the revised collective sale framework and enhanced ABSD remission framework address different constraints in the redevelopment process.

The Land Titles (Strata) amendments deal mainly with the owner side. For older developments, the lower consent thresholds could make it easier to secure the agreement needed for a collective sale once the amendments take effect.

The ABSD revisions deal with the developer side. Longer completion and sales timelines give developers of large and mega sites more room to manage the planning, construction, financing and sales demands of projects at this scale.

The two measures are therefore complementary. Lower consent thresholds may help more ageing large developments reach the market, while longer timelines could make the resulting sites more viable for developers bidding for them.

However, the two frameworks classify developments differently and should not be conflated.

The collective sale consent thresholds depend on the age of the existing development. The ABSD remission timelines depend on the number of units produced after redevelopment, subject to the 1.5-times intensification requirement.

Large residential developments form a small but significant housing pool

SRI Research analysed Singapore’s existing private non-landed residential developments by unit count and age as of 2026, focusing on those with at least 700 units.

SRI identified 71 such projects, totalling 68,070 units. Of these, 65 developments, comprising 58,013 units, have between 700 and 1,399 units, while the remaining six developments, comprising 10,057 units, have 1,400 units or more.

While these developments make up a relatively small pool of residential projects, they contain a substantial number of homes.

Their eventual redevelopment could therefore contribute to rejuvenating Singapore’s private housing stock and, where planning parameters allow intensification, add to housing supply.

However, their scale can also make redevelopment more complex.

A collective sale requires agreement among owners whose housing needs, investment objectives and expectations may differ. Larger sites can also demand substantial acquisition and development capital, while redevelopment may produce hundreds or even thousands of new homes that must subsequently be built and absorbed by the market.

Only four large condos are 40 years or older

SRI Research’s analysis shows that most of Singapore’s larger residential estates are still relatively new.

Of the 71 with at least 700 units each, 34 of the developments, totalling 34,892 units, are less than 10 years old, while 33, comprising 29,420 units, are between 10 and 39 years old. Only four, comprising 3,758 units, are between 40 and 59 years old. None are 60 years or older.

The figures suggest that the lower consent thresholds will have a limited immediate impact on Singapore’s largest residential developments. The four projects aged 40 to 59 years make up about 5.6% of the 71 developments analysed and 5.5% of their 68,070 units.

However, the longer-term implications could be more significant. The 33 large developments aged 10 to 39 years contain 29,420 units, or about 43.2% of the units analysed. As these estates age, more will cross the 40-year mark and become subject to the lower consent threshold.

Four large developments fall within the proposed 70% threshold band

SRI Research’s analysis shows that four completed condos with at least 700 units are aged between 40 and 59 years: Bayshore Park , Mandarin Gardens , Braddell View and Neptune Court . Together, they have 3,758 units.

Under the revised framework, the consent threshold for developments in this age group will fall from 80% to 70% once the amendments take effect.

The reduction could matter most for large ageing developments. Securing agreement among hundreds of owners can be difficult, especially when they differ over reserve prices, replacement housing and the timing of a sale.

A lower threshold does not guarantee that these developments will pursue a collective sale, let alone complete one. It does, however, reduce one hurdle that large ageing projects face in seeking redevelopment.

None of the six developments with at least 1,400 units has reached 40 years of age, according to SRI Research’s dataset.

For now, the lower thresholds are therefore relevant only to developments with 700 to 1,399 units, rather than the largest estates.

Lower consent thresholds ease one barrier but do not remove it

The effect of the threshold reduction becomes clearer when considered against the scale of larger projects.

To illustrate, in a hypothetical 1,400-unit development, lowering the threshold from 80% to 70% would reduce the support needed from the equivalent of 1,120 units to 980, or 140 fewer. If the development reaches 60 years of age and the 65% threshold applies, the equivalent requirement falls to 910 units, or 210 fewer than under the current rule.

In a 2,000-unit development, the equivalent reductions would be 200 and 300 units, respectively.

These figures are illustrative only. Under the amendments, consent is assessed using prescribed measures including share value and strata area, rather than simply by unit count.

The larger the development, the greater the absolute reduction in support represented by the lower thresholds.

None of the six developments with 1,400 or more units has reached 40 years of age, but the lower thresholds will apply to them once they do.

However, a lower threshold does not settle everything. Owners would still need to agree on the reserve price, how sale proceeds are distributed and other terms of the collective sale agreement.

Consent may get easier, but price still decides

Lower consent thresholds alone are unlikely to spark a broad revival in collective sales. For a deal to proceed, owners’ expectations must still align with what developers are prepared to pay.

Developers will continue to weigh acquisition price, allowable development intensity, redevelopment yield, development charges, construction and financing costs, and expected selling prices.

Large sites are especially sensitive to these factors, given the capital involved and the number of units that must eventually be sold.

The framework may therefore open the door to collective sales for some ageing developments, but it does not change the commercial calculation that determines whether a deal is viable.

Its significance may lie less in the sales it enables today than in the longer-term framework it establishes for rejuvenating Singapore’s ageing private housing stock.

Together with the enhanced ABSD remission timelines for large-scale en bloc redevelopments, it points towards a policy framework increasingly addressing the structural challenges of redeveloping large estates.

Policy, however, can only improve the conditions for redevelopment. For Singapore’s largest estates, whether they become the next generation of housing supply will still depend on whether owner expectations, redevelopment potential and developer economics align.

title: Private home prices rise 1.4% despite weakest 3Q new-home sales since 1998: URA flash estimates
article:
URA's flash estimates showed private home prices rose 1.4% in 3Q2026, up from 0.5% the previous quarter.

It marked the eighth consecutive quarter of price gains and the fastest quarterly increase in almost two years, says Christine Sun, chief researcher and strategist at Realion (OrangeTee & ETC) Group. The last time prices rose faster was in 4Q2024, when they increased 2.3%.

“Overall, prices grew faster due to a bigger proportion of private homes sold at a higher price,” says Sun.

Search for the latest New Launches , to find out the transaction prices and available units

For instance, the proportion of private homes, excluding executive condominiums (ECs), sold for at least $2 million rose from 49.2% in 2Q2026 to 53.6% in 3Q2026, according to Realion.

The shift was even more pronounced in the new sale market, where the share of transactions of at least $2 million surged from 52.3% to 71.7% over the same period, Sun notes.

Private home prices have risen 2.8% in the first nine months of 2026.

Landed homes, OCR lead price gains

The main driver of the price increase in 3Q2026 was the landed housing segment, where prices rose 2.8%, following a 2.5% increase in 2Q2026.

Non-landed home prices increased 0.9%, reversing the 0.1% decline in the preceding quarter.

Among the three market segments, the Outside Central Region (OCR) recorded the strongest price growth at 2.2%, reversing a 0.1% decline in 2Q2026. Huttons Asia attributes the increase partly to higher price benchmarks set by projects such as Vela Bay .

Prices in the Rest of Central Region (RCR) edged up 0.2%, following a 1.2% decline in the previous quarter.

Meanwhile, Core Central Region (CCR) prices slipped 0.1%, reversing the 1.8% growth recorded in 2Q2026.

URA private property price index for 2Q2026 vs 3Q2026

Launches and sales fell sharply in 3Q2026

Major condominium projects launched during the quarter included the 212-unit Amberwood at Holland , 380-unit Dunearn House and 499-unit Lentor Gardens Residences .

Two boutique projects, the 20-unit Duet @ Emily on Mount Emily and the 27-unit The Bronze on Boon Teck Road, were also launched during the quarter, according to SRI.

Launch activity was constrained by the Lunar Seventh Month, says Huttons. An estimated 1,100 units were launched for sale in 3Q2026, 38.3% fewer than in the previous quarter and 73.8% lower than a year ago. According to Huttons, this was the lowest number of units launched in a third quarter.

The limited supply of new launches also weighed on developers' sales. Based on Huttons Data Analytics estimates, about 1,100 new homes were sold in 3Q2026, down 48.6% q-o-q and 66.4% y-o-y.

As developers' sales are supply-led, fewer launches led to correspondingly lower transaction volumes, says Mark Yip, CEO of Huttons Asia.

He adds that uncertainty surrounding the US-Iran truce also prompted some buyers to delay their purchases while awaiting greater clarity. The estimated 1,100 new homes sold made 3Q2026 “the lowest number of units sold in the third quarter of the year since 1998”, according to Yip.

Sales down 46.6% in first nine months

In the first nine months of 2026, developers launched an estimated 4,727 units, 46.6% fewer than in the same period last year. An estimated 5,254 units were sold over the same period, down 33.3% year on year.

Huttons estimates private housing demand in the OCR fell 39.2%, partly due to affordability concerns. Demand in the RCR fell 26.3%, while demand in the CCR rose 1.2%.

Across the primary and secondary markets, sales volume totalled about 4,300 units in 3Q2026, down 30% from 6,148 units in the previous quarter.

Huttons says some buyers also paused their purchases as they digested several recent policy changes affecting the housing market, including the removal of the 15-month wait-out period and changes to the Primary 1 Phase 2C allocation framework from 2027.

More launches expected in 4Q2026

Activity could rebound sharply in the final quarter, when several large projects are scheduled for launch.

“The final quarter of 2026 will likely see a noticeable surge in transactions due to the highly anticipated line-up of blockbuster launches,” says Sun.

These include the 570-unit Lucerne Grand, the 1,268-unit Thomson Reserve and the 133-unit The Serra, which will collectively introduce about 2,000 new private homes.

Sun says the 1,268-unit Thomson Reserve could also influence the overall private residential price index in 4Q2026. Located in the RCR, the project is expected to be priced above $2,600 psf.

“The massive volume and premium city-fringe pricing from this project alone may lead to an uplift in the overall private property price index in 4Q2026,” she says.

However, higher interest rates could temper demand. In September, the US Federal Reserve raised its benchmark interest rate by 25 basis points to a target range of 3.75% to 4%, its first increase since July 2023.

“Nevertheless, some buyers may exercise caution as interest rates could continue to rise in the months ahead,” says Sun.

Labour risks, generational wealth

Domestic economic conditions are another risk. Knight Frank Singapore head of research Leonard Tay says “an eye needs to be kept on the labour market”.

While unemployment remains low, retrenchments increased from 3,830 in 1Q2026 to 4,620 in 2Q2026, with layoffs concentrated in sectors such as manufacturing, information and communications, and financial services.

“There is a sense of uncertainty creeping into the labour market with the proliferation of AI-related disruptors in several industries,” says Tay. “Should job security be undermined, prospective homebuyers might hold off on making a purchase and adopt a more cautious wait-and-see posture.”

At the same time, intergenerational transfers of housing wealth are creating another source of demand in the residential market, says Marcus Chu, CEO of ERA Singapore.“We are seeing older homeowners right-size and unlock equity from properties that have appreciated significantly, while some younger buyers receive family support for their first or next home,” he notes.

“It also helps explain why purchasing power has remained relatively resilient even as home prices and affordability pressures have increased.”

For the full year, SRI head of research and data analytics Mohan Sandrasegeran expects private residential prices to increase by about 3% to 3.5% in 2026, broadly in line with the 3.3% increase recorded in 2025.

“We expect price growth to remain relatively measured in the final quarter,” says Sandrasegeran. “A broader pipeline of new launches in 4Q2026 should provide homebuyers with greater choice across different locations and price points.”

title: Italy draws wealthy Chinese property buyers with lifestyle ­and flat tax
article:
Italy is becoming a magnet for wealthy property investors thanks to its high quality of life and flat tax regime, and interest is also on the rise among mainland Chinese and Hong Kong buyers, property agents said.

Rome introduced a flat tax regime nine years ago to attract high-net-worth individuals, with foreign residents allowed to make a flat annual tax payment of EUR300,000 ($434,700) on all their overseas income under the scheme’s latest rules.

This has become a draw for wealthy investors. The number of participants in the scheme has risen from about 3,000 in 2024 to roughly 5,000 currently, according to Knight Frank.

The property consultancy has also seen a surge in the number of prime residential properties sold in Italy, with deals in the first eight months of the year up by about 140% compared with the same period in 2025.

The buyers are currently mainly from countries including the UK, US, Switzerland, France, India and the Netherlands, noted Knight Frank. But “interest in Italy is growing” among Hong Kong and mainland Chinese buyers as well, said Anna Ward, the firm’s international residential research lead.

For Hong Kong and mainland buyers, the tax considerations are a major attraction, though “lifestyle, diversification and long-term wealth preservation tend to be more important considerations”, Ward added.

About one-third of the prospective Italian property deals Knight Frank had in the pipeline for the autumn period were linked to tax-related relocations, the consultancy said in a separate report.

Demand for Italian real estate was also coming from European second-home buyers, as well as international owners seeking to expand their existing Italian holdings across additional destinations, agents said.

“Italy’s flat tax regime … continues to attract globally mobile wealth, with over 60% of prime international enquiries through Knight Frank now driven primarily by tax considerations,” Knight Frank said.

“This reflects a broader evolution in demand, from the introduction of the flat tax, through post-Covid lifestyle shifts, to the removal of favourable tax regimes elsewhere such as in the UK.”

Many non-EU residents relocating to Italy under the flat-tax regime also require visa arrangements, with relocation often going hand in hand with property acquisition and broader investment activity, according to Knight Frank.

The visa is open to non-EU citizens investing in Italian businesses, innovative start-ups, government bonds or philanthropic initiatives. Entry thresholds start at EUR250,000.

Other real estate brokers also expect more buyers from mainland China, Hong Kong and the wider Asia Pacific region to snap up Italian property assets.

Buyer enquiries for Italian real estate more than tripled in the second quarter of the year, compared with the preceding three months, according to property tech firm Juwai IQI, which has seven million property listings across 111 countries.

In the first half of 2026, Italy received the 14th highest number of inquiries from prospective Chinese buyers — ranking between Spain and Vietnam — said Kashif Ansari, Juwai IQI co-founder and group CEO.

The top three were Thailand, Australia and the UK, he added.

“We expect the number of Chinese living and buying residences in Italy to climb in 2027,” Ansari said. “At the top end, the flat tax and residency options are attractive. The Italian market is rising and luxury Italian lifestyle destinations are attracting Asia’s wealthy.”

“Chinese workers find opportunities in Italy’s economy, and nearly one-third of new residency permits going to Chinese citizens are for the purpose of studying in Italy,” Ansari added. “The Chinese are the largest non-EU group at Italian  universities.”

An estimated 290,000 Chinese citizens live in Italy, the fourth largest non-EU community in the country, he said. “Their numbers are climbing rapidly, by up to 8% per year,” Ansari said.

For Lisbon-headquartered Maia Properties, wealthy buyers are looking at Europe as a whole and picking the best base that suits their lifestyle and tax needs.

Although Chinese demand for Italian property is still an “emerging trend”, Luiz Felipe Maia, CEO and founder of the real estate broker, said “there is significant room for it to grow”.

title: New $30.4 mil research programme to develop sustainable construction technologies
article:
A $30.4 million research programme — involving a consortium of Woh Hup, Singapore Institute of Technology (SIT) and A*Star — has been launched to develop sustainable construction technologies and strengthen Singapore’s built environment sector.

This was announced at the Construction Technology Innovation Laboratory’s (CTIL) annual seminar at the SIT Punggol campus on Oct 1.

The three-year programme is supported by the Research, Innovation and Enterprise 2025 (RIE2025) plan, a five-year national plan aimed at strengthening research and development in Singapore.

The programme brings together the three consortium partners and seven other industry partners.

Industry partners will contribute project sites, operational expertise and validation environments to test and refine the technologies under actual construction conditions and accelerate their adoption across the sector.

Chiew Sing Ping, head of CTIL at SIT, noted that the built environment sector is facing increasing pressure to reduce embodied carbon while improving productivity and resource efficiency.

Lim Keng Hui, assistant chief executive of the Science and Engineering Council at A*Star, added: “Addressing sustainability challenges in the built environment requires innovation across advanced materials, engineering and AI-enabled optimisation.”

The programme comprises seven research projects focused on areas such as scaling up ultra-low embodied carbon concrete for wider industry adoption, and developing AI-powered design tools to help engineers optimise structural designs for lower embodied carbon, cost and material use.

By 2029, the consortium aims to reduce embodied carbon in urban development applications of new technologies by up to 40% compared with conventional construction methods.

It also seeks to create new business opportunities and deliver operational cost savings for industry partners.

Beyond research, the programme will support talent and capability development through the training of undergraduate and postgraduate students, as well as applied research opportunities for research staff in collaboration with industry partners.

Industry professionals will also have opportunities to build their capabilities through specialised training, industry attachments and technical seminars.

Yong De-Rhong, executive director at Woh Hup, said: “Our partnership with SIT, A*Star and industry partners gives us the opportunity to co-develop solutions that are not only innovative, but also practical and scalable for the construction industry.”

title: HDB resale prices dip 0.2% q-o-q in 3Q2026, while transaction volumes surge: HDB flash estimates
article:
HDB resale prices fell for a third consecutive quarter in 3Q2026. Flash estimates published by HDB on Oct 1 show that the Resale Price Index (RPI) dipped 0.2% q-o-q, narrowing from the 0.3% fall recorded in the previous quarter.

This came despite an improvement in market sentiment and an increase in housing enquiries following recent policy changes, noted Christine Sun, chief research and strategist of Realion (OrangeTee & ETC) Group.

On July 28, the 15-month wait-out period was removed for private property owners (PPOs) and ex-private property owners (ex-PPOs) buying a non-subsidised resale flat.

“Following the policy adjustment, there was a noticeable increase in buying interest and sales enquiries from private homeowners for HDB resale flats looking to right-size,” said Sun.

Resale transactions totalled 7,528 in 3Q2026, marking a 17.7% q-o-q increase.

Lee Sze Teck, senior director of data analytics at Huttons Asia, remarked: “While the PPOs and ex-PPOs were able to buy larger flats from July 28, the effect on prices was relatively muted in 3Q2026, alleviating concerns over outbidding and potential price surge by this group of buyers.”

HDB RPI and transaction volume

Larger flat types drive resale volume

An uptick in sales for larger flat types attributed to the spike in resale transactions, said Eugene Lim, key executive office of ERA Singapore.

A total of 1,822 five-room flats and 535 executive flats were sold during the quarter, up by 23.7% q-o-q and 39% q-o-q, respectively.

Additionally, million-dollar flat transactions also trended upwards in 3Q2026, with 597 resale flats changing hands for at least $1 million during the quarter. These transactions accounted for 8.5% of total resale flat transactions in 3Q2026.

ERA’s Lim noted: “Demand for million-dollar flats could have been driven by cash-flush private homeowners, who now face fewer barriers to entering the HDB resale market.”

Five-room and larger flats formed the bulk, with 353 transactions, up 24.5% q-o-q from 283 in 2Q2026.

Million-dollar flat transaction volume since 2012

Prices of million-dollar flats similarly increased in 3Q20256, with average prices standing around $1.16 million, 1.1% higher than $1.147 million in 2Q2026.

Additionally, the proportion of million-dollar flat transactions in non-mature estates stood at 11.4% in 3Q2026 — the highest thus far, noted Huttons’ Lee.

The most expensive transaction came from the sale of a five-room flat at The Pinnacle @ Duxton for $1.72 million in September, beating the previous record of $1.7 million set just days earlier.

Resale market to “face headwinds”

Realion’s Sun expects the HDB resale market to face headwinds following the increase in the income ceiling for BTO flats. From August 2026, the income ceiling was raised to $16,000 for couples and families and $8,000 for singles.

“The higher income ceiling would allow some to buy larger or pricier BTO flats, thus diverting more buyers away from larger, higher-priced flats in the resale market,” she added.

That said, Huttons’ Lee noted government changes to the allocation and distance priority for Primary 1 registration under Phase 2C from 2027. Under phase 2C, 60 places will be set aside, up from 40 currently.

In addition, 12 primary schools in Bukit Timah, Newton and Marine Parade will allocate more places to children living more than 2km away. For these schools, half of the places will be reserved for children living within 2km and the other half for those living beyond 2km.

The changes could benefit HDB resale flats in areas such as Bedok, Bukit Batok, Bukit Merah, Bukit Timah, the Central Area, Clementi, Geylang, Kallang/Whampoa, Marine Parade, Queenstown and Toa Payoh that are located near the 12 schools, according to Huttons.

Still, Lee expects the HDB resale market to bottom in 4Q2026.

The 13,484 flats reaching their five-year minimum occupation period in 2026 could see keen interest, with some centrally located and five-room flats potentially fetching at least $1 million.

Huttons projects resale flat transactions to total between 22,000 and 26,000 in 2026, while resale price movement may be between -1% to 1%.

Meanwhile, ERA anticipates resale transaction volumes to hover around 26,000 and an annual price growth between 2% to 5%.

“This aligns with the Government’s aim for a stable and sustainable HDB resale market, characterised by resilient buyer demand and healthy price growth,” said ERA’s Lim.

title: Buyers snap up new Hong Kong flats ahead of likely interest rate rises
article:
Hong Kong developers sold all of the more than 290 new flats they launched over the weekend of Sept 26–27, as buyers looked to lock in mortgages ahead of an anticipated rise in interest rates later this year, according to property agents.

The decision by the city’s major banks to hold rates steady despite the US Federal Reserve’s recent rate increase appeared to have given buyers a push, with many expecting local rates to rise in the coming months, said Derek Chan Hoi-chiu, head of research at Ricacorp Properties.

“A notable number of home seekers are actively entering the market to secure properties ahead of anticipated local rate increases,” Chan said.

On Sept 26, Chow Tai Fook-owned Sky Ace Enterprises shifted all of the 140 apartments it made available on its State Residence project in North Point, agents said.

The properties are a mix of one-bedroom to three-bedroom flats with between 28 sq m (301 sq ft) and 56 sq m (603 sq ft) of floor space. They were offered at discounted prices starting from HK$5.96 million ($970,800).

China Land Resources, meanwhile, found buyers for all 153 apartments at The Sterling II made available on Sept 27, agents said. The flats — ranging from 28.5 sq m (307 sq ft) to 67.8 sq m (730 sq ft) — were also offered at discounted prices of HK$5.43 million to HK$15.01 million.

The southwest Kowloon project also offered 35 flats via tender starting Sept 27.

“Developers are likely to push out launches quicker to avoid interest hike uncertainty,” said Norry Lee, senior director of projects strategy and consultancy at JLL in Hong Kong.

The latest sales performance is likely to provide some relief to the property market, after Hong Kong’s lived-in home prices fell 0.46% in July, halting a 13-month upswing, according to the latest official data.

The index tracking second-hand home prices slipped to 321.5 in July from 323 in June, the first decline recorded in 16 months, Rating and Valuation Department data showed.

The decline came weeks before the recent interest rate increase.

On Sept 17, the Hong Kong Monetary Authority lifted the city’s base rate to 4.25% after the US Federal Reserve had raised its target range to between 3.75% and 4% following its latest Federal Open Market Committee meeting.

The city’s three note-issuing banks did not follow suit. HSBC and Bank of China (Hong Kong) kept their prime lending rate at 5%, while Standard Chartered maintained its prime rate at 5.25%, according to separate statements from the lenders.

The Fed is set to meet again in late October. If it raises its target rate again, that could finally trigger Hong Kong’s lenders to adjust their own rates, analysts said.

“Despite potential upside risks in US interest rates and the likelihood of Hong Kong following suit, prevailing market optimism continues to support transaction activity,” Chan of Ricacorp said.

The timing of the launches also had a positive impact on the sales, according to Lee of JLL.

“Timing matters: with Mid-Autumn Festival this week and the National Day ‘golden week’ next week, developers are keen to catch this window for mainland buyers,” he said.

title: October 2026: 3 Temasek-Backed Blue-Chip Stocks to Watch
article:
Late September kept three
Temasek-backed companies
busy.
Mapletree Logistics Trust
(SGX: M44U), or MLT, went first.
On 21 September 2026, it agreed to sell an ageing logistics park in Shanghai.
A day later,
Seatrium Limited
(SGX: 5E2) doubled its share buyback programme to S$200 million.
Keppel Ltd
(SGX: BN4) followed on 23 September 2026, when it confirmed talks with StarHub over a potential deal involving Keppel’s telco, M1.
Temasek, a global investment company headquartered in Singapore, held about 36% of Seatrium and about 21% of Keppel as at 31 March 2026.
Its deemed interest in MLT comes through
Mapletree Investments
, which Temasek wholly owns, and which in turn owns MLT’s manager.
Can MLT keep its DPU steady while it sells assets?
MLT owns 175 logistics properties across nine Asia-Pacific markets, with assets under management (AUM) of S$13.1 billion as at 30 June 2026.
For the quarter ended 30 June 2026 (1QFY2026/2027), gross revenue rose 0.8% year on year (YoY) to S$178.9 million.
Net property income (NPI) grew faster, up 2% to S$156.4 million.
Distribution per unit (DPU) rose 0.2% YoY to S$0.01816.
A softer yen, won and Hong Kong dollar held back the headline numbers.
Strip those out, and gross revenue and NPI would have grown 2.0% and 3.1% respectively.
Portfolio rental reversion came in at 0.9%, or 2.3% once you exclude China.
Occupancy slipped slightly to 96.4% from 96.9% three months earlier.
So why sell the Shanghai park?
MLT wants to rejuvenate its portfolio.
It bought Mapletree Northwest Logistics Park back in 2008 and will now sell it for RMB323.0 million (around S$61.3 million), matching the property’s 31 March 2026 valuation.
MLT did better in July, when it agreed to sell 39 Changi South Avenue 2 at a 20.3% premium to valuation.
The deal is small, making up about 0.5% of AUM, and the manager expects no material impact on net asset value or NPI.
MLT targets completion by 3QFY2027/2028.
Aggregate leverage stood at 40.5% as at 30 June 2026.
What would an M1 exit mean for Keppel?
Nothing is settled yet, and both companies said a deal may not materialise.
A combination would reduce then number of Singapore’s mobile network operators from four to three, meaning regulatory approval is a hurdle.
Notably, Temasek is a controlling shareholder of StarHub as well.
M1 sits in Keppel’s Non-Core Portfolio for Divestment, which the group wants to substantially monetise by 2030.
That portfolio lost S$375 million in the first half of 2026 (1H2026), driven by legacy rig impairments and the terminated M1 sale to Simba.
Because of this, Keppel’s net profit attributable to shareholders fell 59% YoY to S$154.7 million.
The rest of Keppel tells a very different story.
Excluding the non-core portfolio, net profit rose 25% to S$530 million, while recurring income grew 13% YoY to S$467 million.
Keppel held its interim dividend steady at S$0.150 per share.
Free cash flow is the lifeblood of dividends, so where did Keppel’s cash come from?
Operating cash flow fell to S$96.8 million from S$219.4 million a year ago.
Yet Keppel still reported a free cash inflow of S$570 million, driven largely by S$1.1 billion of divestment proceeds and dividends received.
Borrowings stood at S$11.3 billion against cash of S$2.2 billion.
Keppel has announced about S$1.7 billion of asset monetisation this year, against a full-year target of S$2 billion to S$3 billion.
An M1 sale would help close that gap.
Can Seatrium afford a bigger buyback?
Seatrium
finished its previous S$100 million buyback on 1 September 2026.
The new programme is twice the size, funded from existing cash.
Its share purchase mandate caps repurchases at 2% of issued shares.
The profit line looks impressive.
For 1H2026, revenue rose 4.7% YoY to S$5.6 billion, while revenue from rig building, shipbuilding and conversion grew 17.5% to S$4.2 billion.
Profit attributable to owners surged 158.3% to S$372.9 million, though part of that came from a one-off S$171.7 million gain on disposing of non-core assets.
Cash flow is another matter.
Free cash flow was negative S$11.6 million, an improvement from negative S$31.9 million a year ago.
The main drag was a S$1.6 billion build-up in contract assets, as Seatrium recognised revenue ahead of billings.
Cash stood at S$1.7 billion against total debt of S$2.4 billion, excluding lease liabilities. The new buyback equals about 12% of that cash pile.
Seatrium pays dividends once a year, so it declared no interim dividend for 1H2026.
Management expects FY2026 net profit to come in materially higher than FY2025’s, buoyed by those one-off gains.

A buyback or dividend lasts only as long as the cash behind it.
MLT sells older buildings to buy newer ones, and its tenants’ rent continues to support the DPU.
Keppel and Seatrium lean harder on one-offs.
Divestments supplied most of Keppel’s free cash inflow, and Seatrium is buying back shares before its free cash flow has turned positive.

title: DBS, Singtel and ST Engineering Have Rallied: Which Is Still Worth Buying?
article:
DBS Group Holdings
(SGX: D05) is up nearly 37% year-to-date (YTD), while
Singapore Technologies Engineering
(SGX: S63), or ST Engineering not far behind with a gain of 29%.
Singapore Telecommunications
(SGX: Z74), or Singtel, has had a bumpier ride – its share price was up sharply earlier to reach a record high in March 2026 before pulling back, resulting in a negative 6% YTD return.
All three have posted stellar growth in earnings,
dividends
and cash flow in recent times; the harder question now is which one’s fundamentals still justify buying at today’s prices.
Let’s find out.
DBS: Strong Earnings, But Has the Valuation Caught Up?
DBS’s YTD rally is backed by
strong profitability
for the second quarter of 2026 (2Q2026).
Its return on equity (ROE) came in at a robust 17.9% and was accompanied by a record quarterly net profit of S$3.08 billion, up 9% compared to a year ago.
Steady loan growth of 5% YTD helped buffer the decline in DBS’s net interest margin (NIM) to 1.87% from 2Q2025’s 2.05%.
Encouragingly, fee income of S$1.7 billion represented year-on-year (YoY) growth of 22%, with wealth management continuing to be the standout; wealth management income rose a staggering 41.6% YoY to S$919 million.
Critically, management rewarded shareholders by raising the dividend for 2Q2026 by 8% YoY to S$0.81 per share.
With global interest rates rising, DBS’s NIM may recover, supporting further earnings growth.
DBS trades at a rich valuation of more than 3x book value and roughly 19x forward earnings, while sporting a dividend yield of 4.1%; all these metrics comfortably surpass its historical averages.
The main risks for investors to monitor include NIM compression, any pickup in credit costs, slower loan growth, and simply how much of DBS’s quality has been baked into its current valuation.
Singtel: Can the Transformation Deliver More Upside?
Singtel’s share price climbed for several years, up to a peak in March 2026, because its telco business held up and its regional associates kept growing.
Singtel Singapore earned S$230 million in earnings before interest and taxes (EBIT) for the fiscal quarter ended 30 June 2026 (1QFY2027), down 2% from a year ago.
Optus and NCS carried the growth: Optus’s EBIT rose 14% YoY to A$152 million, while NCS’s EBIT jumped 29% to S$102 million.
Together they lifted Singtel’s overall EBIT by 10% YoY to S$462 million.
Turning to Singtel’s regional associates, their post-tax profit rose 16.1% YoY to S$543 million, led by Bharti Airtel and AIS.
The regional associates’ post-tax profit was roughly two-thirds of Singtel’s S$831 million in underlying net profit (up 27% YoY) during the quarter.
Singtel
has been returning capital to shareholders.
There was a record dividend of S$0.185 per share for FY2026, up 8.8% from FY2025.
The dividend combined a S$0.134 per share core dividend (80% of underlying profit) and a S$0.051 per share value realisation dividend funded by asset sales.
In addition, Singtel has conducted a near-billion-dollar buyback YTD.
But it’s worth noting that the core dividend can only rise as fast as underlying profit, and Singtel’s EBIT is guided to grow by just a low-to-mid single-digit percentage rate in FY2027.
That said, Singtel is in discussions to sell a significant minority stake in Optus, which could provide capital for further value realisation dividends.
Singtel currently yields about 4.3%, while trading at a forward earnings multiple of around 20.
The catch is that Singtel’s dividend has exceeded its earnings in recent periods, with asset sales filling the gap.
Singtel’s main risks include intensifying telecom competition, increased regulatory pressure and execution on its digital transformation strategy.
ST Engineering: The Growth Story Behind the Rally
ST Engineering has increasingly been valued as a growth and income stock rather than a traditional defence contractor, and the numbers support this shift.
Revenue surged 11% YoY to S$6.6 billion for the first half of 2026 (1H2026), with net profit jumping 27% to S$512 million.
ST Engineering’s business is supported by a robust order book of S$35.7 billion as of 30 June 2026.
Free cash flow was healthy at S$628.6 million, or S$0.20 per share, which comfortably covers the dividend of S$0.09 per share for the period.
ST Engineering’s Commercial Aerospace segment continues to ride structural MRO (maintenance, repair and overhaul) demand, while the Defence and Public Security segment benefits from rising government spending under long-duration contracts.
The company’s order book grew 14% YoY in 1H2026, which is faster than its revenue growth.
This gives real visibility into future revenue – although margins  on that revenue are not guaranteed.
ST Engineering trades at a premium valuation of 30x forward earnings, a rich multiple that assumes continued flawless operational execution.

Investors would do well to monitor these developments in the coming quarters: for DBS, its net interest margin; for Singtel, the Optus sale and how proceeds are split between debt and shareholder returns; and for ST Engineering, contract wins and margins.

title: Passive Dividend Boost: 3 SGX Stocks Rewarding Investors in October 2026
article:
Three SGX-listed companies are preparing to reward shareholders with
dividends
this October.
PC Partner Group Limited
(SGX: PCT) leads off with its payment on 9 October 2026, followed by
Civmec Limited
(SGX: P9D) on 23 October 2026, and
Union Gas Holdings
(SGX: 1F2) on 29 October 2026.
These upcoming payouts run the gamut from steady, unchanged amounts to one that has more than doubled.
But as
income investors
know, a declared dividend is only as dependable as the cash backing it up.
Let’s look closer at the numbers to see how each company stacks up.
How did PC Partner more than double its dividend?
PC Partner reported revenue of HK$6.5 billion for the six months ended 30 June 2026, marking a 1.5% year-on-year (YoY) increase.
More impressively, net profit attributable to owners surged 117.9% over the same period to reach HK$545.5 million.
This earnings surge was driven by expanding margins rather than sales volume.
Gross margin widened to 16.5% from 10.5% a year prior, bolstered by rising average selling prices for video graphics array (VGA) cards.
While OEM/ODM VGA card sales jumped 73.9% on more orders for high-end cards, own-brand VGA revenue fell 9.2% as shortages in GPUs and graphics memory trimmed volumes by 18.4%.
On the back of these results, the board declared an interim dividend of SGD 0.10 per share (roughly HK$0.61), up substantially from HK$0.25 a year ago, though no special dividend was declared.
Crucially, this higher payout is firmly supported by cash generation.
Free cash flow surged to HK$2.5 billion from HK$648.7 million a year earlier.
As of 30 June 2026, PC Partner held HK$2.9 billion in cash against HK$1.3 billion in borrowings, putting it in a healthy net cash position of around HK$1.6 billion.
Looking ahead, management expects a more challenging second half as rising graphics memory costs and limited VGA card availability take a toll.
Nevertheless, leadership remains confident in delivering full-year revenue growth for 2026.
Can Civmec sustain its dividend without free cash flow?
For its full year ended 30 June 2026 (FY2026), Civmec saw revenue rise 11.4% YoY to A$903.0 million, while net profit attributable to owners grew 22.5% to A$52.1 million.
Growth was particularly pronounced in the Infrastructure, Marine & Defence segment, where revenue more than doubled to A$210.2 million.
The segment now includes Luerssen Australia (renamed Civmec Defence Industries), acquired on 1 July 2025.
The board declared a final dividend of A$0.035 per share.
Combined with the A$0.025 interim payout, Civmec’s full-year dividend stands at A$0.060 – matching its FY2025 total.
However, free cash flow swung to negative A$28.5 million, down from positive A$56.1 million last year.
Management attributed this dip to increased working capital tied up in heightened business activity and unbilled work in progress.
As of 30 June 2026, the company held A$54.6 million in cash against A$60.0 million in borrowings (excluding lease liabilities), putting it in a minor net debt position.
While Civmec held its total payout steady, operating cash flow in FY2026 was negative, covering neither capital expenditure nor dividends.
On a forward-looking note, a record order book, active tendering, and growing early contractor involvement engagements give the business decent visibility heading into FY2027.
What funded Union Gas’s maiden special dividend?
Union Gas posted a strong 1H2026, with revenue leaping 66.4% YoY to S$106.0 million and net profit surging 175.8% to S$12.0 million.
The main engine behind this performance was the liquid fuel division, which saw revenue jump 444.4% to S$51.7 million on higher sales volume and new contributions from the Dunman Road and Queensway service stations.
By contrast, the gas fuel segment remained flat at S$53.8 million.
Marketing and distribution costs barely moved despite a 66.4% jump in overall sales.
This solid performance led the board to declare an interim ordinary dividend of S$0.0048 per share, matching last year’s level, along with a maiden special dividend of S$0.0032 per share.
This brought total dividends for the half to S$0.0080 per share, up 66.7% YoY.
The payout was well funded by cash, with free cash flow expanding to S$25 million compared to S$1.3 million a year ago.
As of 30 June 2026, Union Gas sat on S$29.3 million in cash against S$7.6 million in borrowings, giving it a comfortable net cash buffer of S$21.7 million.
Management expects to finish FY2026 on a strong note, supported by full-year contributions from Dunman Road and nearly 11 months from Queensway.
Looking further ahead, two additional service stations in Marsiling and Jurong West are slated to open in 2027, expanding its network to five locations.
The group also strengthened its core footprint by acquiring two LPG retailers on 31 July 2026 for S$8.2 million.
Get Smart: How do you tell whether a dividend can last?
At the end of the day,
free cash flow
is the true lifeblood of any dividend.
Civmec maintained its full-year payout of A$0.060 in FY2026, but its free cash flow turned negative as operating cash flow itself was in the red.
On the other hand, Union Gas generated S$25 million in free cash flow, giving it the headroom to reward shareholders with a maiden
special dividend
alongside its regular distribution.
The distinction matters.
When you see a dividend, look past the declared amount.
Ask whether the business generates enough cash to keep those payments coming.

title: October 2026 Reward: 3 Blue Chip Stocks Paying Higher Dividends
article:
DFI Retail Group
(SGX: D01),
Hongkong Land
(SGX: H78) and
Jardine Matheson
(SGX: J36) all raised their interim payouts after reporting improved first-half earnings.
All three belong to the Jardine Matheson group, with
dividend hikes
ranging from 8% to a significant 77%.
However, a bigger payout only counts if the company can comfortably keep paying it.
Let’s examine whether each business has the cash flows to back up these higher distributions.
Can DFI Retail sustain a 77% dividend increase?
DFI Retail
declared an interim dividend of US$0.062 per share for 1H2026, up 77% year on year (YoY) from US$0.035.
No special dividend was declared this time, unlike the US$0.443 special payout declared a year ago alongside a lower ordinary dividend.
This payout boost is supported by improved underlying earnings, which rose 11% YoY to US$117 million.
Excluding the divested Singapore Food business, the closed Mannings China operations and its former minority stake in Robinsons Retail, underlying profit rose 44%.
Underlying operating profit from continuing businesses grew 14%, helped by reduced central overheads and lower net financing charges, which dropped to US$51.6 million from US$69.0 million.
Headline revenue dipped 6% YoY to US$4.1 billion due to business divestments and store closures.
However, underlying revenue from continuing businesses rose 4% YoY, supported by a 3% gain in like-for-like sales.
Free cash flow came in at US$382.7 million, down 9.3% YoY, owing to higher capital expenditure.
Nevertheless, the balance sheet remains in solid condition with just US$22 million in net debt.
Looking forward, management raised its full-year guidance, anticipating organic revenue growth of 3.0% to 4.0% and underlying profit between US$285 million and US$305 million.
Because DFI generates far more free cash flow than its ordinary dividend requires and carries minimal debt, the expanded payout looks well covered, with room for future growth.
Why did Hongkong Land raise its interim dividend by a third?
Hongkong Land
lifted its interim dividend by 33% to US$0.08 per share, up from US$0.06 a year ago.
Underlying profit rose 11% to US$259.1 million, while underlying earnings per share climbed 14% to US$0.1207 on a reduced share count.
Net financing charges dropped to US$56.2 million from US$88.0 million as capital recycling efforts bore fruit.
Operating profit held broadly flat at US$318.9 million.
Higher contributions from LANDMARK and a 43% earnings increase in China Integrated Properties offset the income lost from selling Marina Bay Financial Centre Tower 3 and handing over floors at One Exchange Square.
Free cash flow declined to US$153.2 million from US$207.0 million, mainly driven by a near-doubling in major renovation spending to US$109.3 million.
Despite the lower cash flow, net gearing remained conservative at just 11%.
The group’s capital recycling programme reached US$3.7 billion, representing 93% of its target of at least US$4 billion by end-2027.
Meanwhile, a new retail cluster at Westbund Central, its flagship Shanghai development, opened in May with over 80% committed occupancy.
Management expects full-year underlying profit growth to track broadly in line with the first half.
While net gearing of 11% gives Hongkong Land ample balance-sheet flexibility to maintain this payout level, investors should monitor whether elevated renovation spending continues to constrain free cash flow in upcoming quarters.
What does Jardine Matheson’s 8% increase signal?
Jardine Matheson, the parent company of both DFI Retail and Hongkong Land, declared an interim dividend of US$0.65 per share, up 8% YoY from US$0.60.
Management also provided guidance for a full-year dividend of at least US$2.47 per share.
Group revenue fell 7% YoY to US$15.9 billion, but adjusted underlying profit rose 9% to US$735 million.
Higher contributions from Jardine Pacific, Hongkong Land and DFI Retail, alongside lower group financing costs, helped offset an 8% decline in Astra’s contribution to US$358 million.
Astra was hit by tougher conditions in its Mining Solutions and Heavy Equipment segment and a weaker Indonesian rupiah.
Performance at Jardine Pacific included US$24 million in non-recurring lease remeasurement gains.
Free cash flow declined 23% YoY to US$1.5 billion.
As of 30 June 2026, the group held US$7.5 billion in cash against total borrowings of US$14.8 billion (excluding lease liabilities).
In addition to the dividend increase, the group launched a new US$500 million share buyback programme and expects to close its US$2.4 billion acquisition of I-MED Radiology Network in 4Q2026.
Guiding for a minimum full-year dividend signals management’s confidence in the group’s cash generation.
However, with free cash flow down 23%, the I-MED acquisition and the new US$500 million buyback will compete with dividends for cash.
Get Smart: Don’t Treat Group-Wide Dividend Hikes as a Monolith
When dividend increases sweep across a parent company and its subsidiaries, it can look like a uniform signal of strength throughout the entire conglomerate.
However, each listed entity must fund its distributions from its own operating cash flows.
Before assuming a parent company’s payout is completely assured, look under the hood to confirm that each listed entity must fund its distributions from cash it actually receives or generates.
It is equally important to track major capital commitments – such as large acquisitions – that could compete with dividend payouts for available cash in the quarters ahead.

title: BYD export strength offsets tepid home demand again in September
article:
(Oct 1): BYD Co’s vehicle sales rose by 17% in September as the world’s largest electric-vehicle manufacturer extended a run of export growth to offset dwindling demand in its home market.

BYD sold just over 460,000 vehicles last month, according to a statement on Thursday, bringing the total for the year to 3.13 million, a decline of 4% compared with the same period in 2025. The company has an annual sales target in a range of five million to 5.5 million.

Overseas sales accounted for just below 40% of the September total as BYD’s expansion in Europe, Southeast Asia and South America gathers pace. With the Iran war pushing up oil prices, European drivers are increasingly turning to EVs or plug-in hybrids, two categories in which BYD has a wide array of offerings.

Europe is a particularly important market, where consumers are relatively open to EVs and have higher spending power. BYD aims to build three vehicle assembly factories and one EV battery plant in the region over the longer term and has held talks to explore acquiring underutilised factories in countries including France, Spain and Italy.

The picture isn’t so rosy at home, with domestic sales continuing to fall compared with last year. The sector is struggling with shrinking government EV subsidies and a prolonged property crisis that has sapped consumer spending.

title: Microsoft’s trillion-dollar quarter shows AI trade won’t quit
article:
(Oct 1): With Microsoft Corp’s best quarter for decades in the books, Wall Street is betting the stock can keep rallying as the tech giant’s standing in the artificial intelligence (AI) landscape continues to improve.

The shares jumped 37.5% from July through September, their best quarterly showing since 1998, adding US$1 trillion ($1.28 trillion) to the company’s market capitalisation. Microsoft also was the fifth-best performer in the technology-heavy Nasdaq 100 Index, which has gained just 0.4% over the last three months.

“After a period where it struggled with the message, Microsoft has been crisper and cleaner on how it will monetise its capital outlay and benefit its customers,” said Chad Morganlander, a senior portfolio manager at Washington Crossing Advisors and a long-time holder of the stock.

Much of the surge came after Microsoft’s earnings in late July, which showed the fastest cloud growth in four years from strong AI demand. The stock jumped 16% the next day, its best session since October 2008, adding US$450 billion in market value.

The report eased concerns about whether Microsoft’s heavy AI investments would lead to better growth, which is notable because the company has a more encouraging financial profile than the other big spenders like Alphabet Inc, Amazon.com Inc and Meta Platforms Inc. Of the four, Microsoft is the only one that hasn’t seen free cash flow turn negative on an annual basis.

See also: DeepSeek unveils Huawei AI chip tools that may replace Nvidia’s

“It is showing a clear path to profitability with AI,” Morganlander said. “As a company that is spending but not going into the red on account, it looks like the adult in the room.”

Microsoft’s rally is particularly impressive considering the speed of the reversal in sentiment. June was the stock’s worst month since 2000, as investors questioned the company’s spending and the overall outlook for software companies in an AI world. But those industry concerns have eased, and investors were encouraged by the company’s effort to transform its Copilot AI assistant into a product for corporate customers.

“There are still fears of a ‘SaaSpocalypse’, but it seems like Microsoft is less vulnerable to those issues,” Morganlander said. “Meanwhile, people are impressed with how Copilot has been adopted and integrated.”

See also: Trump backs independent AI audits in shift of safety posture

That said, while this quarter’s push has carried Microsoft into the green for the year, its 6.1% gain significantly trails the Nasdaq 100’s 20% surge.

“It ripped this quarter because people made a mistake,” said JoAnne Feeney, a portfolio manager at Advisors Capital Management, which owns Microsoft shares. “Investors realised they misunderstood the company’s potential, so a lot of the rally is just the reversal of that mistake.”

Still, the improving optimism has made Microsoft a darling on Wall Street. There are 72 analysts tracked by Bloomberg who follow the company, and only three don’t have 'buy' ratings. No one rates it a 'sell'. And the average target price suggests the shares will rise about 11% in the coming 12 months.

Last week, Stifel upgraded the stock to 'buy' because Microsoft had “clearly turned the corner”, according to analyst Brad Reback. The stock’s momentum should continue in the second half, he wrote, noting that he’s “increasingly comfortable with the company’s ability to sustain mid/upper teens revenue growth”.

Microsoft shares could generate a total return of roughly 20% over the next year, according Morgan Stanley’s Adam Wood, who pointed to its long-term growth potential and the company’s recent decision to raise its dividend.

“Combined with high-teens EPS (earnings per share) growth, this supports a durable high-teens total return profile at Microsoft, framing an attractive risk/reward,” Wood wrote in a note dated Sept 16.

Revenue is expected to rise 18% in Microsoft’s 2027 fiscal year, which closes at the end of June, roughly in line with fiscal 2026. Wall Street expects that figure to hit 21% in fiscal 2029. And while earnings per share is expected to climb about 11% in this fiscal year, down from nearly 32% in fiscal 2026, it’s projected to reach nearly 19% in fiscal 2028 and 21% in fiscal 2029.
